cases.title: Caching per-user authorization decisions with TTL expiry

result.recommendation: Keep the Redis read-through cache direction, but (a) reduce TTL to seconds and add eager invalidation from the existing `permission-events` topic (it is already published; consuming it adds no API dependency), and (b) solve the miss tail: at an 85% hit rate, 15% of requests still pay ~180 ms, so p95 stays in the miss bucket (~180 ms) and the 120 ms budget is missed. With misses above 5% of traffic, p95 is defined by miss latency, not hit latency — the ~40 ms estimate is arithmetically unsupported.
critical_assumptions: Production hit rate will be ≥95% (not 85%), otherwise p95 remains ≥180 ms
Log-replay locality matches live traffic distribution
A 15-minute stale allow after HR removes an account or group membership is an acceptable (and compliance-tolerable) security window
permissions-service.check outcome for a given key is stable enough that caching the boolean is safe
Redis cluster has memory/headroom for the working set at 2,500 rps peak
material_risks: Security: removed employees retain document access for up to 15 minutes; HR offboarding is explicitly a stated driver of writes, so this is the most likely real damage
p95 budget not met: 15% misses at ~180 ms puts p95 well above 120 ms; the stated ~40 ms target confuses average/median with p95
Unshare/share in the web UI visibly fails for up to 15 min, generating support load and loss of user trust in the sharing controls
Cache stampede on cold keys: 12 pods × concurrent misses hammer permissions-service simultaneously, reproducing the original tail
False confidence from a feature-flag rollout that only measures hit-rate/latency, not staleness or revocation correctness

falsification_probe.description: From 1 h of live request logs, compute the actual (userId, docId, action) reuse rate at 15-min and at ~30 s windows, and derive: miss_rate = 1 - hit_rate. If miss_rate > 0.05, estimate p95 as miss-latency (~180 ms). One SQL/awk pass over sampled GET /documents/:id logs.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: miss_rate ≤ 5% at the chosen TTL AND production locality ≥ 95% confirms the proposal's p95 claim; miss_rate ≥ 10% or locality materially below 85% falsifies it and forces invalidation + miss-tail handling before rollout.

result.recommendation: The cache direction is right, but the p95 math is wrong: a 15% miss rate puts the 95th percentile inside the miss population, so p95 stays at roughly miss latency (~220 ms), not ~40 ms. Add Kafka-driven invalidation from the existing `permission-events` topic (it already exists; you just need a consumer) so revocations are near-immediate, and combine a short-TTL L1 in-process cache plus in-flight request coalescing (singleflight) to push the effective miss rate below 5%. Re-run the log replay with a p95 target, not a mean-hit-rate target, before rollout.
critical_assumptions: The 85% log-replay hit rate generalizes to live traffic key distribution across 12 pods and 2,500 rps
Stale allow decisions for up to 15 minutes after an unshare or HR account removal are acceptable to security/compliance
A boolean decision is context-independent — no group-membership or document-attribute inputs that change without a per-doc write
`permission-events` messages carry enough key data (userId, docId, action) to map to cache keys
The Redis cluster absorbs ~2,500 reads/s plus writes without becoming the new p95 bottleneck
material_risks: Quantitative: 85% hit rate ⇒ 15% of requests pay the ~180 ms miss, so p95 ≈ 200+ ms and the 120 ms budget is missed despite the cache working as designed
Security: revoked access (terminations, unshares) remains valid for up to 15 minutes; cached `allow` outliving a termination is a real breach scenario
Invalidation requires a reverse index (user→keys, doc→keys) or prefix scans; scanning a Redis Cluster across slots at 2,500 rps is expensive and easy to get wrong
Thundering herd/stampede on cold or expired popular keys at 12 pods, amplifying load on the already-slow permissions service
Group-membership removals do not naturally map to `authz:{userId}:{docId}:{action}` keys, silently serving stale group-derived allows
result.better_alternative: Kafka consumer on the existing `permission-events` topic for targeted invalidation, layered as: singleflight-coalesced in-process L1 (2–5 s TTL) → Redis L2 (moderate TTL as safety net) → permissions-service on miss. The L1 plus coalescing exploits real-time request locality that log replay underestimates and is what actually drives the miss rate under 5% needed for p95.

falsification_probe.description: Write a ~50-line script that replays the 24 h access log through a TTL-cache simulator, charging 40 ms per hit and 220 ms per miss, and reports the simulated p95 for 15-min and 2-min TTLs (also with a 2 s L1 layer).
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Falsified if simulated p95 ≥ 120 ms at any TTL (expected: ~200+ ms at 15 min), confirming the hit-rate target is insufficient; confirmed only if p95 < 120 ms.

error.message: Reviewer response invalid after one repair retry: it was not a valid JSON object

result.recommendation: Keep the read-through Redis cache but add a Kafka consumer on `permission-events` that deletes affected `authz:*` keys, and drop the TTL to 60-120s as a backstop against missed events. 15-minute TTL alone allows up to 15 minutes of stale allow after unshare or HR offboarding, which is a security regression; the stated goal is latency, not maximal hit rate. Instrument stale-allow and invalidation-lag metrics alongside hit rate before widening beyond 10% traffic.
critical_assumptions: permissions-service.check is a pure function of (userId, docId, action), so a cached boolean is valid
permission-events is published for every share/unshare/group/HR removal — if it isn't, no amount of TTL tuning fixes revocation lag
stale allow for up to 15 minutes after unshare or account removal is acceptable to security/compliance
log-replay hit rate of 85% reflects production key distribution under the same TTL
Redis has headroom at ~2,500 miss-mixed ops/s with this key cardinality
material_risks: Stale allow for up to 15 minutes after unshare or HR offboarding: a terminated employee retains document access — the exact failure mode identified as critical
No invalidation consumer means correctness rests entirely on TTL; a Kafka delivery gap silently extends staleness to 15 minutes with no detection
Cache stampede when a hot key expires or on pod rollout, spiking permissions-service load at peak and blowing the 120ms p95 on miss paths
Cache stampede/dogpile on the top-doc keys: 85% hit rate still leaves ~375 rps of misses concentrated on hot documents
Dashboards cover hit rate and latency but not staleness, so a silent security regression ships green

falsification_probe.description: From the 24h access-log replay dataset, join each document-access event against share/unshare and HR-removal events, and compute the distribution of time between (a) unshare/offboard and (b) the last subsequent cached-allow hit that the 15-min TTL would have served.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If p95 stale-allow window exceeds the agreed revocation SLO (assume ~60s), the 15-min TTL design is falsified regardless of latency gains; if nearly all revocations fall outside the replayed access window, staleness risk is low and the proposal stands as written.

result.recommendation: The read-through cache direction is right, but a 15% miss rate puts p95 on the miss path (~180ms + overhead), so the 120ms budget will not be met; serve stale entries with asynchronous refresh (stale-while-revalidate) or otherwise bound the slow tail so misses never dominate p95. Also consume the existing `permission-events` Kafka topic to invalidate (or proactively delete) `authz:{userId}:{docId}:*` entries on share/unshare/revoke, otherwise revocations propagate only after the 15-minute TTL — an unacceptable staleness window for an HR deprovisioning flow. Finally, bound cache size/eviction policy so the authz keys cannot evict session keys in the shared Redis cluster.
critical_assumptions: Aggregate 85% hit rate holds for the tail of users/docs that actually drive p95 (hit rate may be skewed toward hot documents)
Cached boolean decisions are correct and complete — no context-dependent checks (IP, time, elevation) that make the decision non-reusable across requests
Redis cluster has headroom at 2500 rps to absorb ~2500 gets/s plus writes without impacting session latency
permissions-service.check latency (~180ms) is not itself fixed, so the miss path remains over budget
permission-events messages are ordered/reliable enough to be used for invalidation
material_risks: Stale allow for up to 15 minutes after unshare or account removal — a security and compliance incident, since the HR integration explicitly removes memberships
p95 remains above 120ms because misses are 15% of traffic and sit above the 95th percentile
Authz cache keys evicting session data (or vice versa) in the shared Redis cluster, causing logouts or session thrash
Boolean cache hides permissions-service changes; no invalidation path means a bad write (or bug in permissions-service) is frozen for 15 minutes across 12 pods
Thundering herd on expiry: a hot key expiring causes 12 pods to concurrently call permissions-service, spiking p99

falsification_probe.description: Simulate the latency distribution: replay the 24h log-derived cache trace through a model where hits cost ~5ms and misses cost ~180ms (permissions-service p95) at the observed 85/15 split, and compute resulting p95 — or simply inject a 15% synthetic miss rate into a staging deployment and read p95 off the latency histogram.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If modeled/staging p95 > 120ms (expected, since 15% misses put p95 on the miss path), the 'p95 should drop to ~40ms' claim is falsified and stale-while-revalidate or sub-5% miss rate is required; p95 ≤ 120ms would confirm the proposal as written.

result.recommendation: Keep the read-through Redis cache with TTL but add (a) a Kafka consumer on permission-events to delete affected keys so share/unshare and HR revocations propagate in near-real-time with TTL as backstop, (b) single-flight/stampede protection per key and a small jitter on TTL to avoid synchronized expiry, and (c) a shorter TTL (or no caching) for high-risk actions if the consumer is unavailable. Roll out behind the flag with hit-rate, p95, and cache-staleness dashboards, and validate the 85% hit rate against real traffic rather than log replay alone.
critical_assumptions: Boolean decision is a pure function of (userId, docId, action) with no request-context dependence.
Security/compliance accepts up to 15 minutes of staleness for revocations when no invalidation event is processed.
Log-replay hit rate (85% at 15 min) matches production traffic mix.
Shared Redis cluster has headroom for ~2,500 rps authz reads/writes without hurting session traffic.
Miss-path p95 (check + network) fits within 120 ms budget when only ~15% of requests miss.
material_risks: 15-minute TTL-only staleness: HR terminations and unshares remain valid for up to 15 min — a real security/compliance incident.
Cache stampede on rollout, Redis flush, or failover floods permissions-service at peak rps, degrading upstream and other consumers.
Hit-rate overestimate from log replay: if actual hit rate is materially lower, p95 exceeds the 120 ms budget.
Hot keys or memory pressure on the shared Redis cluster degrade session traffic sharing the cluster.
Cached boolean hides context-dependent decisions, granting access the live service would deny.

falsification_probe.description: Replay 24h of real traffic (not sampled logs) through an offline simulator computing hit rate for (a) 15-min TTL only vs (b) 15-min TTL + invalidation on permission-events; separately benchmark p95 latency of a cold check() call from a pod to permissions-service.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the TTL-only hit rate on real traffic is materially below ~85%, or cold check() p95 is such that even 15% misses exceed 120 ms budget, the proposal as written is falsified; if hit rate holds and miss-path fits budget, the proposal is confirmed (modulo the staleness concern, which the probe won't cover).

result.recommendation: Keep the Redis read-through cache, but subscribe the document service to the existing `permission-events` Kafka topic and delete `authz:{userId}:{docId}:*` keys (or otherwise mark them stale) on every relevant write, instead of relying on a 15-minute TTL alone. Drop the TTL to ~30–60s as a safety net, add per-key in-flight locks with jittered TTLs to prevent 12-pod stampeding on hot misses, and define a fail-open/fail-closed behavior (plus circuit breaker to permissions-service) for Redis outages.
critical_assumptions: Cached 'allow' for up to 15 minutes after an unshare or HR-driven account/group removal is acceptable to the security/compliance owners
`permission-events` carries enough identity (userId, docId, group/membership changes) to locate affected cache keys, and the cache key shape can be invalidated by it
Decisions are effectively boolean and do not embed per-request context (IP, time-of-day, resource attributes) that would make the key incomplete
Redis cluster has headroom for ~2,500 rps of authz reads plus writes, and session traffic won't be degraded
Log-replay hit rate (85%) generalizes to peak-hour traffic and to the shorter TTL you actually run
material_risks: Stale authorizations: a user retains access to an unshared document, or an offboarded employee retains access, for up to 15 minutes — a direct security/compliance incident, the exact scenario the HR integration exists to prevent
Ignoring the already-published Kafka events wastes the one invalidation mechanism provided by the owning team; TTL-only eviction is unbounded staleness by design
Thundering herd: on a hot-key miss all 12 pods call permissions-service simultaneously, partially undoing the latency win and risking a permissions-service overload at 2,500 rps
Cache-stampede/latency during Redis failover or slow episodes could push p95 above the 120 ms budget with no defined degrade path
Poisoning across shared keys if `userId` or `docId` values are not uniformly formatted, causing cross-user decision leakage
result.better_alternative: Consume `permission-events` from Kafka to actively invalidate `authz:{userId}:{docId}:{action}` keys on every share/unshare/membership change, paired with a short (30–60 s) TTL purely as a backstop — this preserves the decoupling claim while bounding staleness to seconds rather than 15 minutes.

falsification_probe.description: Run the log-replay simulation twice, once with a pure 15-min TTL and once with event-driven invalidation + 60s TTL: measure hit rate, p95 estimate (miss_rate * 180ms + overhead), and 'staleness window' — the delay between a permission-revoking event and cache eviction — sampled against real share/unshare and HR-removal events.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If staleness windows >5–10s exist for revocation events, or the invalidated-cache hit rate falls far below ~70% (making p95 >120 ms), the proposal as written is falsified; if staleness is bounded and hit rate holds, it is confirmed.

result.recommendation: Keep the read-through Redis cache but shorten TTL to 60-90s and add a Kafka consumer on permission-events to delete affected keys on write, using TTL only as a safety net. Also add cache stampede protection (short jitter or per-key lock) and an explicit revocation-staleness SLO on the dashboards alongside hit rate and p95 latency.
critical_assumptions: permission-events publishes reliably on every share, unshare, group change, and account removal
15 minutes of stale 'allow' after an HR offboarding is acceptable — the proposal asserts decoupling as a benefit without stating a staleness bound
Log-replay hit rate of 85% predicts live hit rate at the real key distribution
Redis cluster serving sessions has headroom for ~2,500 rps authz reads plus writes
permissions-service latency is service-internal, so caching (not pooling/locality) is the only lever available this quarter
material_risks: Up to 15 minutes of cached 'allow' after an account or membership is removed — a security/compliance incident if offboarding requires faster revocation
Cache stampede when popular keys expire simultaneously, thundering permissions-service past peak 2,500 rps and worsening the very p95 being fixed
Degraded authz keys writing transient permissions-service errors into cache as durable denials (negative-result caching of failures)
Redis contention degrading session performance for all users sharing the cluster
Feature-flag rollout tracking hit rate and latency but not staleness, so correctness regressions go unnoticed

falsification_probe.description: Send a synthetic permission-events message for a user whose document decision is already cached (seed Redis key authz:{userId}:{docId}:{action}), then observe how long the cached 'allow' remains valid, and separately query the permission-events producer's code/logs to confirm an event is emitted on account removal and group membership change.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If no event fires on offboarding, or cached decisions persist up to full TTL after an event, the proposal's decoupling claim is safe only because it ignores revocation — falsifying soundness of TTL-only. If events fire within seconds and product accepts 15-min staleness, the proposal stands as-is.

cases.title: Retyping and renaming a column on a 900M-row table

result.recommendation: Keep NUMERIC as the target type, but do not run ALTER ... TYPE directly: integer→numeric is not binary-coercible, so PostgreSQL must rewrite all ~900M rows while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which will stall the 1,200 writes/s peak and likely run for many minutes to hours. Instead add a nullable amount_minor NUMERIC(19,3), backfill in batches under the migration role with lock_timeout/statement_timeout per batch, dual-write both columns, cut reads over in a deploy, then add NOT NULL/constraint and drop the old column later. Also drop or defer the RENAME: it executes in the pre-deploy job, so the old pods still running during the ~25-minute rollout will query a nonexistent column and fail checkout for that whole window.
critical_assumptions: The ALTER ... TYPE completes quickly enough to avoid blocking writes (it does not: it forces a full table rewrite).
PostgreSQL DDL atomicity means safe rollout — atomic only wrt rollback, not wrt lock duration or old-code compatibility.
The rename can happen before pods are replaced without breaking running instances of the current code.
Night-time write volume (~150/s) leaves enough headroom for a multi-minute exclusive lock, and replicas can replay the resulting WAL without falling behind.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the correct scale for 3-decimal currencies (KWD/BHD/OMR need scale 3; 4 was not justified) and existing reporting SQL casts/compares still work.
material_risks: Full rewrite of a 410GB table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks all reads/writes on orders, breaching the 99.95% checkout SLO.
Column rename lands pre-deploy while ~25 minutes of old pods are still live: every orders read/write from old code raises UndefinedColumn, an outright outage.
Two large DDLs replay on both streaming replicas, potentially stalling WAL apply and causing replica lag/failover risk.
Three raw-SQL reporting jobs break silently at cutover if not updated in lockstep.
Migration job may run for hours with no statement_timeout, blowing past next Tuesday's release window.
result.better_alternative: Expand/contract pattern: add amount_minor NUMERIC(19,3) nullable → batched backfill (COPY-style UPDATEs in chunks with lock_timeout=500ms and retries) → app dual-writes and reads new column → enforce NOT NULL + CHECK in a later release → drop amount. This avoids the rewrite lock entirely and gives an in-window rollback.

falsification_probe.description: On a staging clone (or a scaled-down table with tens of millions of int rows), time `ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4);` while a concurrent session runs a simple SELECT/INSERT, and sample `pg_locks`/`pg_stat_activity` wait events during it.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the ALTER takes more than a few seconds or the concurrent session waits on 'Lock'/'relation', the proposal's atomic-and-fast assumption is falsified; a sub-second result with no blocking would support it.

result.recommendation: Drop the in-place ALTER TYPE + RENAME on a 900M-row hot table; the full rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock is incompatible with the 99.95% SLO and the pre-deploy migration timing. Either (a) keep INTEGER and store thousandths with a per-currency scale factor, no DDL, shipped Tuesday, or (b) add a new NUMERIC(19,3) amount_minor column, backfill online in throttled batches, dual-write, cut over, and drop the old column later. Do not rely on 'DDL is transactional' as a safety argument — atomicity does not bound lock duration.
critical_assumptions: That ALTER TYPE from INTEGER to NUMERIC completes quickly enough not to block readers/writers materially (it will rewrite every row)
That the pre-deploy migration job's exclusive lock will not outlive or stall the 25-minute rolling deploy
That existing INTEGER values fit a 10x-reduced range under a thousandths encoding (max amount headroom)
That all three raw reporting queries and any index/constraint/logical-replication consumers are updated atomically with the rename
That 'nighttime low traffic' still tolerates minutes of total write+read stall within the monthly 99.95% budget
material_risks: Minutes-long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocking all traffic on the primary, breaching the SLO and likely the release window
Migration job holds the lock while old pods still serve traffic; those requests hang until statement_timeout or deploy finishes
Replica apply lag spikes during the rewrite, delaying failover readiness
Rename cutover mismatch: pre-replace pods still writing 'amount' fail after DDL, causing a partial-failure window
Atomic-rollback misconception: rollback also requires completing the rewrite, so 'rolled back' does not mean fast
result.better_alternative: Encode thousandths in the existing INTEGER column (scale factor in currency metadata) for the Tuesday release — zero DDL, zero lock risk — and schedule any NUMERIC normalization as a later, backfilled, dual-write change.

falsification_probe.description: On a staging clone of the 900M-row table, run the exact migration statements with pg_locks monitored: `BEGIN; SET lock_timeout='5s'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); ...` timed, and separately run `EXPLAIN`-less timed full rewrite equivalent (e.g., `CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT amount::numeric(19,4) FROM orders;`) to measure rewrite cost.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Rewrite completing in a few seconds = proposal viable; rewrite taking minutes/hours or lock_timeout expiring repeatedly = falsifies the proposal and confirms REPLACE.

result.recommendation: Do not ALTER TYPE on the 410GB orders table: on PostgreSQL an integer->numeric conversion forces a full table rewrite under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which will stall checkout writes well beyond the night window and flood WAL into the replicas. Instead add a new amount_minor BIGINT (or NUMERIC(19,3)) column, dual-write in the release, backfill existing rows in throttled batches, then cut the three reporting queries over. The proposal also never rescales existing values, which is a silent data-corruption bug, not just a schema change.
critical_assumptions: That ALTER COLUMN TYPE on 900M rows completes without blocking writes for a material time (it rewrites the whole table)
That existing integer cents values can be reinterpreted at the new scale without any rescale step
That application writes after the change use the same numeric magnitude as pre-existing rows
That replication lag from a 410GB rewrite will not stall the reporting jobs or replica-served reads
That no other ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock holder (autovacuum, pg_repack, another migration) collides with the rewrite
material_risks: Full table rewrite holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for minutes-to-tens-of-minutes: checkout writes block, breaching the 99.95% SLO (only ~19 min/month of budget)
Rewrite generates massive WAL, spiking replication lag on both streaming replicas and stalling the reporting jobs
No data rescale: pre-existing values are off by 100x (or 10x) relative to newly written rows, producing silently wrong revenue figures
Mixed-scale rows during the 25-minute rolling deploy as old pods write cents while new pods write the new scale
NUMERIC(19,4) neither matches the 3-decimal requirement nor retains INTEGER write throughput at 1,200 writes/s
Transactional DDL gives atomicity, not non-blocking: the transaction commits or rolls back, but everything waits on the lock while it runs
result.better_alternative: Add a new amount_minor column, dual-write from the app, backfill existing rows in batched/throttled increments (rescaling 2-decimal currencies to thousandths), verify, then drop the old column in a later release. This avoids the rewrite entirely and gives a clean rollback path before Tuesday.

falsification_probe.description: On a production-sized clone (or restored backup) of orders, run: BEGIN; SET lock_timeout='5s'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; ROLLBACK; — timing it and capturing pg_locks / pg_stat_activity wait events during the statement.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the ALTER takes more than a few seconds or any session shows a wait on the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, the night-window/atomicity claim is falsified and the rewrite is unsafe; a sub-second result (impossible at 410GB) would support it. Corroborate by checking SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE amount needs rescaling (mixed-magnitude check).

result.recommendation: Split the migration into expand/contract: first add a nullable amount_minor (or rename in a separate release after code is updated), and replace the single ALTER TYPE rewrite with a throttled backfill or at minimum measure the rewrite's duration/WAL/lag first. Run the type change with a statement_timeout, lock_timeout, and lag guard even under the migration role, and guarantee a mixed-version compatibility window across the 25-minute rolling deploy (view/alias or dual-column). Update all reporting SQL and confirm no other readers of orders.amount exist before cutting over.
critical_assumptions: A single ALTER TYPE on 900M rows finishes fast enough at ~150 writes/s to fit the pre-deploy job without breaching replica lag, WAL, or disk limits.
The pre-deploy migration fully completes before any old pods are replaced, so no pod runs mixed code/schema.
NUMERIC(19,4) is semantically correct (existing values are integer cents, converted to 4-decimal numerics without unit confusion downstream).
The three reporting jobs are the only readers of orders.amount and can be changed in the same release.
Off-peak night traffic in the deploy's time zone is truly the global minimum (no other region/batch job peaks then).
material_risks: Full-table rewrite generates hours of WAL and long locks: replica lag spike, replication slot exhaustion, disk fill → SLO breach despite DDL atomicity.
Rolling deploy's 25-minute mixed-version window breaks if rename/type change lands before all pods are replaced → 42P01/42804 errors in production.
Migration role has no statement_timeout: a hung rewrite blocks the pre-deploy job indefinitely and stalls the release.
Reporting raw SQL silently off by 1000x for KWD/BHD/OMR if rename or scale change isn't matched in all consumers.
NUMERIC storage/index bloat and ORM Decimal regressions vs BIGINT minor units.
result.better_alternative: Expand/contract: ADD COLUMN amount_minor (BIGINT minor units), dual-write, throttled backfill with replication-lag and lock_timeout guards, then atomic swap/rename in a later step once reports and readers are updated — this avoids the 900M-row rewrite entirely and fits the SLO.

falsification_probe.description: On a full-size copy (or a representative partition), time `ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4);` under the migration role while simulating ~150 wps, recording duration, WAL bytes generated, replication lag delta, and lock wait.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the rewrite completes in minutes with bounded WAL/lag and no lock timeout, the single-migration proposal stands; if it takes hours, spikes lag past SLO, or blocks writes, the proposal is falsified and expand/contract backfill is required.

result.recommendation: Do not rewrite 900M rows in Tuesday's pre-deploy job. Instead add `amount_scale SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 2` (catalog-only, fast), gate KWD/BHD/OMR writes behind a feature flag that scales the integer by the currency's ISO 4217 exponent, and defer any full rescale to a later throttled backfill outside this release.
critical_assumptions: A single ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE rewrite of 410GB fits in the 25-minute pre-deploy window
The pre-deploy migration job completes before pods are replaced; otherwise the deploy proceeds against a table mid-alter
NUMERIC conversion preserves integer→numeric mapping that all three raw SQL reporting queries and ORM filters expect
Replication lag and WAL during the rewrite stay below levels that would trip the 99.95% SLO
`amount_minor` rename can be applied atomically to code that reads `amount` via raw SQL without a coordinated dual-read window
material_risks: Full-table rewrite of 900M rows at 1,200 writes/s peak causes prolonged ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and huge WAL; replica lag spikes and reporting queries fail against the standby, breaching the SLO
Transactional DDL only guarantees atomicity, not duration: if the job runs long, the rolling deploy continues and pods come up against a half-migrated or not-yet-migrated schema
Raw SQL reporting queries referencing `orders.amount` break at rename time if not all three are updated in the same deploy and cannot be hot-fixed without another migration
NUMERIC(19,4) is wider than needed and slower than integer for range scans on an indexed column; index size grows on the 410GB table
Rollback after a successful rewrite means a second 410GB conversion back to integer, which cannot fit in Tuesday's window

falsification_probe.description: On a restored or representative 10-50M-row slice of `orders`, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE plus timed `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4)`, and extrapolate lock duration and WAL generated to the full 900M rows while a concurrent 1,200 writes/s load runs.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If extrapolated rewrite time exceeds the pre-deploy window or causes replica lag > replication_max_allowed_before_drop, the proposal is falsified; if it completes in minutes with negligible lag, KEEP becomes viable.

result.recommendation: Keep amounts as INTEGER in the smallest currency unit (minor units, i.e. thousandths for KWD/BHD/OMR) and interpret scale per currency in the model/serializer layer. If a schema change is truly required, do an additive migration: add amount_minor NUMERIC(19,3) NULL, backfill in batches under a lock-tolerant job, dual-write, then swap during the deploy window. The proposed ALTER+RENAME must not ship.
critical_assumptions: ALTER TABLE ... TYPE on 900M rows / 410GB rewrites the table (and any index on amount) while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, taking far longer than the 25-minute deploy window
The migration runs in the pre-deploy job while old pods are still serving traffic, so the RENAME COLUMN breaks running code before replacements land
The three reporting jobs and any views/ORM queries reference the column name 'amount' and are not all redeployed atomically with the migration
All existing order rows are non-negative integers that fit the new semantics, and no downstream consumer parses amount as 'cents'
Low-traffic (night) still means ~150 writes/s queued behind the lock, plus analytics readers
material_risks: Full-table rewrite holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for minutes-to-hours, stalling 150/s writes and analytics reads; a multi-minute stall exceeds the ~21 min/month budget implied by 99.95% SLO

RENAME COLUMN lands in the pre-deploy job before pods are replaced: every running pod and the three raw-SQL reporting jobs get 'column amount does not exist' for the duration of the 25-minute rolling deploy
NUMERIC(19,4) records a scale of 4, not the 3 decimals these currencies actually use; downstream code that divides by 10000 vs 1000 will silently misprice KWD/BHD/OMR orders
Rollback after a partial consumer rollout (some code expecting amount, some amount_minor) is not transactional at the application level even if the DDL is

Replace it with an atomic conditional UPDATE inside a transaction (UPDATE ... WHERE code=$1 AND redeemedAt IS NULL RETURNING id, treat 0 rows as AlreadyUsed) so correctness is enforced by Postgres across all replicas. Keep the concurrent-request test, but run it against two separate processes or via direct SQL race to actually exercise cross-pod contention.

A single-row UPDATE with a WHERE guard is atomic under Postgres MVCC (it is)
chargeOrder can tolerate being ordered after or rolled back relative to the claim (needs an explicit decision)

Replace it with an atomic conditional claim in Postgres: `prisma.coupon.updateMany({ where: { code, redeemedAt: null }, data: { redeemedAt: new Date(), orderId: order.id } })` and throw AlreadyUsed when `count === 0`, deciding explicitly whether to claim before chargeOrder (with a compensating release on charge failure) or after (accepting a failed-charge-then-rollback path). cases.title: Rewriting billing logic across five services in one cut-over

result.recommendation: Abandon the 3-month billing-v2 branch and single cut-over PR; instead build a golden-invoice characterization suite from current production outputs first, then extract billing-core and migrate plan-by-plan behind feature flags with dual-run comparison, deleting each plan's legacy path as it proves parity. Keep the clean domain model and thorough unit tests from the proposal, but deliver it incrementally on main so equivalence evidence accumulates continuously rather than arriving in one unreviewable PR at month three.
critical_assumptions: Invoice equivalence for all 37 plans can be verified from data available before the rewrite (fixtures exist or can be captured in production).
A 3-month branch across 5 services can be reconciled with ~40 external PRs/week with tolerable conflict cost.
The team can fully re-specify 6 years of proration rules from code reading without behavioral feedback from production.
A single mega-PR touching 5 services and deleting old code is reviewable and safely rollback-able.
Notification ordering, payment retries, and tax call timing are observable only via invoices and thus covered by invoice comparison.
material_risks: Branch rot: 13 weeks of divergence across 5 actively-changed services produces a merge that rewrites or breaks other teams' merged work.

Silent invoice drift: with 22% happy-path coverage, golden expectations written during the rewrite will encode the team's guesses, not legacy behavior — grandfathered plans are the least-tested and most likely to be wrong.
All-or-nothing cutover: defects surface only in production billing with no per-plan rollback; financial damage and trust loss are immediate.
Single reviewable-less PR: correctness depends on reviewers catching subtle proration changes across 14k LOC, which will not happen.
Cut-over stall: no dual-run evidence means the team cannot know when billing-core is actually equivalent, so the branch never merges.

result.recommendation: A 3-month branch with a single big-bang merge is unworkable against ~40 unrelated PRs/week touching these services. Instead, extract billing into billing-core incrementally behind the existing interfaces: lock behavior first with characterization/golden-invoice tests over all 37 plans (22% happy-path coverage cannot guarantee identical invoices), route one service at a time via strangler-style seams with dual-run/diffing of old vs new invoice output, and land continuously. Reserve the new day-granular plan model as a feature flag added once parity is proven.

No other team will change billing services meaningfully during a 3-month fork, or merges back will be trivial.
The new domain model can be validated against legacy output without a dual-run comparison harness.
Grandfathered (11) plans' behavior is captured by tests rather than tribal knowledge.
One PR can be reviewed safely despite deleting old code across 5 services and 14k LOC.

Single giant PR is effectively unreviewable, defeating the point of a review gate at highest-risk moment.
Deleting old code immediately removes the ability to diff or roll back.
Team of 3 blocked for 3 months with no incremental value delivered.

The day-granular plan capability lands as new data the model already supports, so the actual objective is achieved early instead of at month 3.

result.recommendation: Reject the single big-bang branch and 3-month cut-over: at 22% coverage with no equivalence oracle, a one-shot cutover of 37 plans (11 grandfathered) across 5 services has no way to prove invoices are unchanged except code review. Replace it with: build a golden-invoice characterization harness first (replay historical invoices through current code), then extract rules into a declarative plan schema evaluated in one place, migrating plan-by-plan behind feature flags with production shadow-mode invoice diffing. cases.title: Adding a composite index concurrently for a slow query (sound control)

result.recommendation: Keep the composite (account_id, created_at DESC) CONCURRENTLY non-transactional migration — that's the right access path — but prefer the partial variant `WHERE status <> 'void'` if the query predicate is stable, and explicitly test EXPLAIN on a 2M-row enterprise account before rollout since post-filter scans on huge accounts may still miss p95. Also add monitoring for INVALID indexes (pg_index.indisvalid) and confirm no existing duplicate index before creating, and note CONCURRENTLY still takes ShareUpdateExclusiveLock briefly.
critical_assumptions: The 2.5s is entirely due to the missing composite access path, not to heap fetch or network costs
created_at ordering within an account is what the app actually needs (no timezone/collation surprises)
The status predicate in the query is stable enough that a partial index (if chosen) wouldn't become stale
No existing index already covers (account_id, created_at) — proposal doesn't check for duplicates
CONCURRENTLY build time on 60M rows fits within an off-peak window and replication lag stays acceptable
material_risks: Failed/CANCELLED CONCURRENTLY leaves an INVALID index silently, wasting space and confusing future reviews
Enterprise accounts (2M rows) may still require scanning many index entries to find 20 non-void rows if void rows cluster by created_at — partial index mitigates this
CONCURRENTLY still takes brief ShareUpdateExclusiveLock waits; at 150 writes/s some writes could queue momentarily
Redundant index if an equivalent index already exists, doubling write amplification
Off-peak assumption may be wrong for a global customer base

falsification_probe.description: On a staging clone with the same schema, run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = <largest_ent> AND status <> 'void' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;` after creating the index, and check `SELECT indisvalid, indisready FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.indexrelid WHERE c.relname LIKE 'idx_invoices%';`
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the plan shows an Index Scan with actual rows fetched ≈ 20 (not millions) and low buffer counts, and indisvalid=true — confirms. If it still shows a large index scan with hundreds of thousands of rows read, or indisvalid=false, the proposal is wrong/incomplete.

result.recommendation: Keep the composite (account_id, created_at DESC) CONCURRENTLY index as the core fix, but add: (1) a pre-build safety check to confirm created_at is NOT NULL and the query's DESC ordering matches the index exactly; (2) an explicit monitoring plan for replication lag with an abort threshold during the build (since writes must not be blocked/stalled beyond a few seconds); (3) an explicit step to verify the largest accounts (2M rows) return via index descent with no large sort, not just that the planner 'uses an index'; (4) a plan to query pg_index.indisvalid and drop INVALID indexes on failure (already mentioned but make it a pre-step too, since a prior failed attempt leaves clutter); (5) run ANALYZE on invoices after build to refresh stats before the p95 comparison.
critical_assumptions: created_at is NOT NULL and immutable per row so the (account_id, created_at DESC) index fully satisfies ORDER BY ... DESC without a nulls sort
Migration tool's disable_ddl_transaction actually wraps only this statement, allowing CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction block
RDS replication/WAL can absorb a 60M-row concurrent build without exceeding the few-second write-impact budget
Planner will choose the new index after ANALYZE; stats correlation for account_id is representative
No existing INVALID index with same name exists from a prior failed attempt
material_risks: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY fails partway (deadlock/lock timeout/lag abort), leaving an INVALID index that must be detected and dropped before retry — the proposal mentions this but does not make detection a pre-step
Replication lag spikes during the multi-minute build on 60M rows, violating the 'writes not blocked for a few seconds' constraint (lag stalls apply/commit indirectly)
Largest accounts (2M rows) may still sort many index entries if created_at ties or NULLs force non-index ordering
Post-build plan may still be a seq scan if stats are stale, hiding the regression
WAL/IO pressure during off-peak build still overlaps with 150 writes/s baseline on shared storage

falsification_probe.description: On a clone or with a hypothetical index, run: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = <largest_account> AND status <> 'void' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; also check SELECT indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indexrelid = 'idx_invoices_account_created'::regclass; after build, and monitor rds_metric_queries / pg_stat_replication replay_lag during build.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Falsify: Index Scan node that does NOT stop at ~20 rows (rows removed by sort, or Sort node with large input), OR pg_index.indisvalid = false, OR replay_lag exceeding a few seconds during build. Confirm: Index Scan with actual=20 rows and tiny buffers, indisvalid=true, lag within budget.

result.recommendation: The composite (account_id, created_at DESC) index is the right fix, but harden the build: set lock_timeout=1s and a statement_timeout (or run it as a supervised one-off, not a raw migration statement) so CONCURRENTLY can't hold the start/end SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE locks or block, and monitor pg_stat_progress_create_index plus replication lag. After the build, run ANALYZE on invoices (RDS autovacuum may lag after a long concurrent build), then verify plans for both a typical account and the 2M-row enterprise accounts, and drop any INVALID index before retrying. Consider adding status as a third key column or a partial index only if the post-filter shows measurable overhead in EXPLAIN BUFFERS.
critical_assumptions: CONCURRENTLY in a non-transactional migration is allowed by the RDS IAM/role and the migration runner executes it outside any transaction block (some tools wrap statements anyway).
pg_stat_progress_create_index and pg_stat_replication/lag metrics are visible to the operator on this RDS instance.

created_at is effectively unique/stable enough that ordering ties won't cause nondeterministic page churn, and the column has a default now() with correlated-enough distribution to avoid skewed index scans.
The 2M-row enterprise accounts don't have a large fraction of void rows that would make the post-filter plus LIMIT 20 scan far more than 20 index entries.
Statement-level lock waits during the build won't trip an existing application lock_timeout/statement_timeout in a way that aborts user queries.
material_risks: CONCURRENTLY build failing midway (deadlock, owner session drop, deadlock_timeout) leaves an INVALID index; retrying without first DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY causes the same failure again.

Long build at 150 writes/s (~hours on 60M rows with default maintenance_work_mem) increases WAL volume and replication lag on the RDS replica, breaching the no-downtime/availability constraint indirectly.
Post-build bloat and stale stats make the planner keep choosing a seq scan, so p95 doesn't improve despite the index existing.
Holding locks at the start/end phases longer than 'a few seconds' if a long-running transaction blocks the concurrent build's waits, stalling DDL.
The migration being non-transactional means a partial failure leaves schema state that the migration tool may re-run unsafely on the next deploy.

falsification_probe.description: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) 'SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = <largest-enterprise-account-id> AND status <> \'void\' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20' on a replica after the index exists, and also query: SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indexrelid = 'idx_invoices_account_created'::regclass;
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Falsified if the plan is still a Seq Scan/Sort, if rows removed by filter is ~2M (post-filter consuming the LIMIT badly), if actual rows returned from the index scan vastly exceed ~20-40, or if indisvalid = false. Confirmed by an Index Scan (or Index Backward Scan) with 'Rows Removed by Filter' small and execution in single-digit milliseconds.

result.recommendation: The composite (account_id, created_at DESC) index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a non-transactional migration is the right fix and satisfies the no-downtime constraint. Strengthen it by setting a short lock_timeout/statement_timeout for the build, checking pg_stat_activity for long-running transactions before starting (CIC waits on old snapshots and can stall), and confirming the INVALID-index cleanup path with `SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;`. Optionally verify planner choice on both a small account (index scan) and a 2M-row account (scan that stops at 20).
critical_assumptions: disable_ddl_transaction is honored so CIC is not wrapped in an implicit transaction block.
created_at is not volatile/updatable in a way that makes ordering semantics differ from a seq scan; ties are acceptable.
A plain btree on (account_id, created_at) suffices — no need to also index/filter status since void rows are <1%.
RDS permits running a long CIC build and the maintenance/off-peak window is long enough for 60M rows.
The application tolerates ~1-3% extra write amplification and index storage for one more index.
material_risks: CIC failing halfway leaves an INVALID index consuming write overhead and planner space until dropped and retried.
A long-running open transaction (analytics/replication slot) blocks CIC completion indefinitely, keeping extra locks held longer than a few seconds.
Replication lag spike during the build on RDS could trigger failover or push replicas past failover thresholds.
Blocking waits at the start/end of CIC can briefly delay the 150 writes/s workload if the build is retried during peak.
Post-filter on status plus ties on created_at may return slightly different row sets than the old seq scan, surfacing as pagination bugs.

falsification_probe.description: After the build, run: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = <largest_enterprise_id> AND status <> 'void' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Replication slot/lag headroom can absorb a multi-GB index build on 60M rows
The enterprise accounts (2M rows) are not the p95 driver — otherwise heap fetches during the sort still hurt
RDS allows CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (superuser-equivalent via rds_superuser) and no logical-replication conflict blocks it
The visibility map will keep index-only scans viable if we add INCLUDE (status)

falsification_probe.description: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with a representative enterprise account_id (≈2M rows) after index creation, using SET enable_seqscan = off if needed to force the planner to consider it.

created_at ordering lets the planner stop after 20 rows via index scan even for 2M-row enterprise accounts.

CONCURRENTLY build on 60M rows finishes within the replication-lag budget at 150 writes/s.
Fresh statistics (ANALYZE) will make the planner choose the new index rather than a bitmap/seq scan.

Replication lag spikes during the two-scan build, breaching the 'writes not blocked for more than a few seconds' constraint or triggering RDS failover.
Implicit transaction block wraps the statement, causing immediate failure mid-migration and partial deployment state.
Planner misestimates status <> 'void' selectivity or created_at correlation and picks a plan that still sorts all matching rows for large accounts.

falsification_probe.description: On a staging replica with a scaled-down but similarly distributed invoices table, run: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_test ON invoices (account_id, created_at DESC); then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = <largest_account_id> AND status <> 'void' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Planner will choose the new index after ANALYZE for both small and 2M-row accounts (stats fresh, no generic-plan regression)

Replication lag spike during a 60M-row concurrent build breaches the write-stall constraint or causes replica query timeouts

Enterprise accounts still show a large sort/heap-fetch step if created_at values within an account are not effectively ordered in the index as scanned, keeping their p95 high

cases.title: Replacing RabbitMQ with Redis Pub/Sub for job dispatch

result.recommendation: Redis Pub/Sub cannot provide the at-least-once delivery, manual ack, redelivery-on-restart, or DLQ semantics the system already depends on, so it must not carry payment-provider webhooks or fulfilment triggers. Replace it with Redis Streams using consumer groups (XADD/XREADGROUP/XACK/XAUTOCLAIM) plus trimming, lag alerting, and a retry/DLQ path, and roll it out first to low-risk job types (thumbnails, search indexing) while keeping RabbitMQ for payment traffic until the new path is proven. Do not decommission the RabbitMQ cluster after only a one-week dual run.
critical_assumptions: Jobs published while a worker is being redeployed several times per day will be durably retained and redelivered
The in-worker retry wrapper can only retry messages it successfully received, so pre-receive losses are unrecoverable
AOF everysec plus failover RPO of up to ~1 second is acceptable for order-paid events (it is not)
Consumers of payment webhooks and fulfilment require at-least-once delivery with idempotency, not best-effort
Publishers will not block or receive backpressure when subscribers lag or crash
material_risks: Silent message loss during pod restarts or brief network blips drops payment webhooks, leaving orders unpaid with no retry or DLQ evidence
No ack/redelivery means the existing 5-retry DLQ guarantee silently disappears, so failures become invisible rather than paged
Lagging or OOM-crashed subscribers accumulate unbounded server-side buffers instead of back-pressuring publishers, hiding overload until memory exhaustion
The one-week dual-run plus decommission destroys the fallback before Redis-based dispatch is proven under real failover and upgrade conditions
Double-publishing during overlap without tested idempotency keys triggers duplicate fulfilment or duplicate emails
result.better_alternative: Redis Streams with consumer groups reusing the already-operated Redis (no new managed service, satisfying the budget freeze), which restores durable at-least-once delivery, acks, crash recovery, and a DLQ-equivalent while still removing the RabbitMQ upgrade treadmill; migrate low-risk job types first and keep RabbitMQ for payment webhooks until Streams passes failover and lag testing.

falsification_probe.description: Kill a SUBSCRIBING worker pod (kubectl delete pod) mid-stream, then publish 1000 jobs of that type from a loop, restart the pod, and count how many jobs were eventually processed versus published; repeat with AOF fsync everysec and a forced failover (redis-cli DEBUG SLEEP / cluster failover) while publishing.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Falsified if fewer than 1000 jobs are processed (Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget and will drop all messages published while no subscriber is attached, plus any lost to AOF failover). Confirms the proposal only if 100% of jobs survive pod restart and failover with no duplicates causing double fulfilment.

result.recommendation: Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget and cannot meet your existing delivery guarantees: nothing is persisted, there are no acks, no consumer groups, and no DLQ, so any message published while a worker is restarting, scaling, or crashing is silently lost. Replace it with Redis Streams (already in your Redis 7 deployment) using consumer groups, XACK, and XAUTOCLAIM/XREADGROUP with a pending-entries claim loop to reproduce retry + DLQ semantics, or keep RabbitMQ and reduce burden via infrastructure automation (Terraform/Ansible-managed upgrades, alerts on quorum/queue alarms, an operator-managed cluster) instead of changing the messaging model.
critical_assumptions: AOF persistence durably stores Pub/Sub messages (it does not; Pub/Sub data is never written to AOF/RDB)
The in-worker retry wrapper can preserve at-least-once delivery when the broker gives no redelivery mechanism
Workers are always connected at publish time despite several redeploys per day and autoscaling
Sub-millisecond latency and 300 msg/s throughput are the binding requirements (they are not; reliability is)
Running both paths for a week lets you safely decommission RabbitMQ without proven loss statistics
material_risks: Silent message loss during worker redeploys, pod evictions, OOM kills, and network blips — directly hits payment-provider webhooks, i.e. lost 'mark order paid' events and unfulfilled orders
No DLQ or retry counting: poison messages either loop forever in-process or vanish, losing the current 5-retry isolation
In-process retry wrapper cannot redeliver a message the process never received or crashed before acking
No backpressure: Pub/Sub pushes at publisher rate, so a slow consumer gets unbounded client-side buffering then dropped messages
