falsification_probe.description: Script a contract test: fetch GET /v1/orders/{id}, all list endpoints, an empty list, an error body, and any webhook fixture; walk the JSON tree, collect every field named `id*`/`*_id*` with a numeric value, assert an exact string sibling exists, then run each response body through Node `JSON.parse` and assert `String(parsed.id) === parsed.id_str`.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any numeric ID field without an exact string twin, or any `id` ≠ `id_str` after JSON.parse round-trip, falsifies the proposal's coverage claim; all green confirms it.

result.recommendation: Keep the parallel `id_str` approach but add a single shared serialization point (or a schema-level assertion) so `id_str` is emitted for every order ID including nested refs, errors, and pagination, backed by contract tests. Mark `id` as `deprecated: true` in the OpenAPI spec with a JS-specific warning, publish the regenerated SDKs in the same release train as the web app switch, and gate rollout on a response-schema audit confirming full coverage.
critical_assumptions: Mobile iOS/Android parsers today succeed on large numeric IDs, so the breakage is JS-only and additive string fields don't need a mobile fix
The ~40 partner SDK generators support additive string properties and can be redistributed within two weeks
The web app can switch to `id_str` in the same release as the API, making the lockstep fix immediate
Adding a field is API-compatible under current versioning and no consumer pipeline requires `id` to remain a JSON number
The API has a shared serialization layer where `id_str` can be added once rather than per-endpoint
material_risks: Incomplete `id_str` coverage on some endpoints or nested objects leaves a live corruption path and forces ad-hoc client branching
Partners continue reading numeric `id` indefinitely; deprecation without enforcement means corruption persists indefinitely
Numeric `id` remains present, so newly onboarded JS consumers copy the broken pattern from examples/docs
Mixed client code that displays `id` but echoes `id_str` (or vice versa) reintroduces Number coercion bugs
Partner SDK regeneration slips past the two-week window, leaving integrations on schemas without `id_str`

falsification_probe.description: Diff the OpenAPI response schemas (or run a contract test over every order-carrying endpoint and nested/error object) listing every field named `id` or `*_id` and verify each has a sibling `_str` string field emitted at runtime.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any order-ID field without a corresponding string sibling falsifies coverage completeness; full pairing confirms the core mechanism holds.

result.recommendation: Adding an additive string field is the right call given old mobile builds must keep parsing a numeric `id`, so do not switch `id` in place. But strengthen three things: (1) make adoption measurable via explicit SDK/API-version request headers or a documented telemetry signal rather than user-agent sniffing, which cannot tell you which field a consumer reads; (2) add a JS/TS SDK-side guard that logs or throws on lossy parse of `id` so silent corruption is surfaced for the long tail that misses the changelog; (3) explicitly document that strict schema validation on partner side must tolerate the new property, and add a contract test asserting `id` is byte-identical to today (no precision change) and that path/query params accept both forms.
critical_assumptions: iOS (Codable) and Android (Moshi) tolerate unknown extra fields, so adding `id_str` does not break un-updated mobile builds.
Changing `id` itself to a string would break the ~weekly-release mobile installs still in the wild, which is why in-place stringification is off the table (this justification is never stated).
The two-week window covers web deploy + SDK regeneration/publish, not partner re-integration — the numeric `id` will keep corrupting JS consumers who do not migrate, indefinitely.
No consumer uses strict schema validation that rejects unknown properties.
Existing path/query handling already accepts digits as strings, so 'accept both forms' is a no-op rather than new work.
material_risks: Silent, permanent data corruption for any JS consumer that never reads the changelog: `id` remains a lossy JSON number, so a deprecation note is the only defense for the long tail.
User-agent-based adoption metrics are unreliable (proxies, bots, stripped headers) and cannot reveal whether a partner actually switched to `id_str`.
Additive field may break partners with strict request/response schema validation or golden-file tests.
Regenerated SDKs add a second ID field to every model, doubling ID-related surface and inviting inconsistent picks across clients.
Docs-only deprecation of `id` conflicts with keeping it authoritative in the data model, creating ambiguity about which field is canonical for writes/lookups.

falsification_probe.description: curl -s https://<api>/v1/orders/<id-of-a-new-order> | node -e 'let d="";process.stdin.on("data",c=>d+=c).on("end",()=>{const j=JSON.parse(d);console.log("parsed:",j.id,"exact:",String(BigInt(j.id))===String(j.id))})' — compare the parsed value to the real ID from a server-side DB query.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If `exact` is false / parsed != real ID, the corruption premise holds and the additive fix is necessary; if every returned ID parses exactly (all <= 2^53), the stated problem is not real for current data and the proposal's urgency is misjudged.

result.recommendation: Dual-field `id_str` is a valid non-breaking transition and I keep that direction, but the two-week deadline means it must be paired with (a) immediate web-app switch to `id_str` (the proposal has this), and (b) an explicit deprecation timeline plus a server-side guarantee that `id` keeps its current lossy numeric form only for compatibility. Additionally, the OpenAPI spec must document `id_str` as `type: string` with a snowflake pattern so regenerated SDKs produce string-typed models, not `integer` — verify the codegen output. Also state clearly that partners who cannot regenerate yet must read `id_str` manually from raw JSON; do not claim the fix reaches them passively. Consider whether the numeric `id` can be dropped from new-version responses sooner than "a future v2" to avoid a permanent two-source-of-truth state.
critical_assumptions: iOS Int64 and Android Long models continue decoding the numeric `id` unchanged (no strict-schema validation that would reject an added field)
Partner SDK generators tolerate an added response field without breaking compile-time contracts
Web frontend can be redeployed atomically with the API within the two-week window
The OpenAPI change actually causes regenerated SDKs to expose `id_str` as a String type rather than a loose variant
Nested order references exist and are enumerated exhaustively (the proposal assumes a complete inventory)
material_risks: New JS consumers who only read `id` remain silently broken; deprecation in a changelog does not fix data corruption for them
Incomplete enumeration of nested order-bearing fields leaves some paths still emitting only numeric IDs
Two canonical IDs drift apart under future serializers (one path writes only one field)
Partners that auto-map all `_str` suffixed fields inconsistently, or that ignore the new field, keep decoding truncated numbers
If codegen emits `object`/`any` for `type: string` pattern fields in some languages, the mobile/partner models stay weakly typed

falsification_probe.description: Regenerate one representative partner SDK (e.g., TypeScript or Java) from the modified OpenAPI spec with `id_str: {type: string}` alongside numeric `id`, and inspect the emitted model; then run `JSON.parse` on a sample response in Node and confirm `id_str` round-trips to the exact 64-bit value while `id` does not.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the regenerated model types `id_str` as string and Node round-trips the exact digits while `id` shows 1234567890123456720, the proposal is sound; if codegen drops or weakly types `id_str`, or if adding the field breaks existing model consumers' compile, the proposal needs modification.

cases.title: Transactional outbox for reliable event publishing (sound control)

result.recommendation: Keep the outbox, but fix relay concurrency: two pods can lock two different rows for the same order simultaneously and publish them out of order, breaking the per-order ordering guarantee. Serialize publication per key (e.g. single in-flight batch, or route each aggregate_id to one relay instance, or hold the row lock until the send future completes and send batches in strict per-key order), and on partial batch failure mark only the acked rows. Also avoid holding a DB transaction open across the Kafka send, and make created_at/ordering monotonic (DB sequence), not wall clock.
critical_assumptions: The outbox insert happens in the same JDBC transaction as the order insert (same datasource, no REQUIRES_NEW bug).
Consumers actually key their dedup store on the outbox UUID and receive it as the event id (stated, but not verified across all three consumers).
created_at ordering is monotonic across 6 replicas (clock/sequence), so ORDER BY created_at matches logical order per aggregate.
Kafka producer uses idempotence + acks=all so at-least-once relays do not create reordering, and consumers are at-least-once (offsets committed after processing).
Holding row locks / an open transaction across a Kafka send does not trip idle_in_transaction_session_timeout or exhaust the pool during a broker outage.
material_risks: Concurrent relays publishing two events for the same order key out of order -> fulfilment/email act on stale state despite dedup (dedup does not fix ordering).
Broker outage + 'SELECT ... FOR UPDATE' held during send -> lock pileup, connection exhaustion, cascading order-service latency across 6 replicas.
Partial batch ack failure: marking the whole batch published loses events (violates the objective); re-sending the whole batch is safe only if dedup is confirmed.
published_at set only after ack, but no retry/backoff or poison-row handling -> a permanently failing row (bad payload) stalls or repeatedly blocks batches and triggers false alerts.
7-day purge deleting rows is fine for published rows, but any bug path that deletes unpublished rows silently reintroduces lost events.

falsification_probe.description: Integration test: 2+ relay instances, artificially slow/faulty Kafka producer, insert two outbox rows for the same order_id ~50ms apart, record arrivals at a consumer that logs (event_id, arrival order); repeat 1000x. Also run a broker-down soak to inspect open transactions/locks.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any consumer observing event N+1 before N falsifies the ordering claim; any unpublished row purged or row marked published without an ack falsifies at-least-once; growing idle-in-transaction sessions during broker downtime falsifies the lock-holding design.

result.recommendation: Keep the outbox direction but tighten three specifics: (1) mandate that no code path can call kafkaTemplate.send for order events other than the relay (lint/grep all send call sites, including the currently buggy path), (2) specify claim/lease semantics for the poller so multiple replicas using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED plus a published_at update in the same session can't double-mark or starve rows, and (3) confirm the 7-day retention job never deletes rows still unpublished (condition deletion on published_at IS NOT NULL). Optionally note that CDC/Debezium is an alternative if polling load becomes a concern.
critical_assumptions: Payload for the outbox row is fully available at commit time within the order transaction
Consumers persist processed event IDs at least as long as the maximum replay/duplicate window
All existing kafkaTemplate.send("orders", ...) call sites will be removed or redirected through the relay
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED polling across 6 replicas is acceptable load on Postgres at the actual order rate
published_at is set only after broker acks (acks=all) and duplicate sends are tolerated by consumers
material_risks: A residual direct-send path bypassing the outbox reintroduces both the rollback-phantom and pod-kill-loss bugs
Retention job deleting unpublished rows during an outage causes silent, permanent event loss
Relay crash between Kafka ack and published_at update produces duplicates — safe only if every consumer's dedupe is truly durable and keyed on outbox id
Polling every replica without a lease/claim can cause starvation or excessive DB load under lag
Ordering per order relies on the relay never concurrently publishing two rows for the same aggregate_id; SKIP LOCKED alone doesn't guarantee this across in-flight batches

falsification_probe.description: Grep/AST-scan the order-service codebase for all kafkaTemplate.send call sites and check whether the rollback-prone code path still exists alongside the outbox; also run `SELECT count(*) FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL` during a controlled broker outage and verify it drains without loss after recovery.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any non-relay send call to the orders topic, or any unpublished row that disappears without a corresponding consumer-visible event, falsifies the proposal as specified; zero bypass sends and full drain-with-dedup confirms it.

result.recommendation: Keep the app-level outbox relay direction, but fix ordering: SELECT ... ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 with SKIP LOCKED across 6 replicas lets a lagging replica publish row N after another replica has already published row N+100 for the same order. Serialize per aggregate (e.g. skip rows whose aggregate_id has an in-flight row, or partition by hash(aggregate_id) into ordered lanes), order by a BIGSERIAL sequence instead of created_at to avoid timestamp ties, and explicitly delete the legacy kafkaTemplate.send() code path from the in-transaction route rather than leaving it as an assumption.
critical_assumptions: The legacy in-transaction send() path is fully removed, not merely bypassed by new code
A stable, unique event id is persisted with the outbox row so a crash between publish and published_at update yields a duplicate the consumers' stored IDs can absorb
Relay uses producer enable.idempotence with acks=all (or explicit retries) so partial broker failures don't silently drop batches
Consumers tolerate out-of-order events per order, or per-order serialization is added
At least one order-service pod is running for the relay to make progress — pods restarting do not stall the backlog indefinitely
material_risks: Cross-replica batch interleaving breaks per-order ordering; fulfilment acting on 'order placed' after a later status event is a real data hazard
Ties on created_at produce nondeterministic ordering even on a single replica
If published_at is set before the ack in any rewrite, the original 0.05% loss silently returns
Unbounded backlog under a full consumer/broker outage: 100-row polling may lag far behind, and the 1-minute alert fires continuously without indicating which direction to fix

falsification_probe.description: Insert ~1000 outbox rows across ~10 aggregate_ids, then run two concurrent poller transactions (two psql sessions or two pods) doing the exact SELECT ... ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, capture the aggregate_id sequence each session acquires, and check whether any aggregate's rows can be acquired/committed out of order across sessions.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If two sessions can hold interleaved rows for the same aggregate (session A holds seq 1 while session B holds seq 2 and commits first), per-order ordering is not guaranteed — confirms the need for per-aggregate serialization. If acquisition is strictly ordered per aggregate, the proposal stands as written.

result.recommendation: Keep the outbox, but do not hold the row-locking transaction open across the Kafka send: claim a batch (set a claimed_at/attempt column) in a short FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED transaction, commit, publish, then set published_at. Specify ordering handling: with concurrent relays, two events for the same order key can be claimed by different pods and published out of order, so route the batch by key or serialize sends per key within a batch. Also define retry/backoff for failed sends (rows must remain published_at IS NULL), a poll interval that actually meets the 'few seconds' budget, and a published-row retention that is shorter than consumer dedup-ID retention.
critical_assumptions: Each order produces at most one event, or events for one order are never published concurrently by different relays
kafkaTemplate.send futures are awaited in claim order so same-key events hit one partition in order
Consumers' processed-event-ID stores retain IDs longer than the 7-day outbox retention and are not pruned/aggregated
Poll interval + batch size keep p99 lag under a few seconds at current order volume with 6 replicas
Claim/published bookkeeping can be done in the same PostgreSQL instance/transaction as the order (same DB, no XA)
material_risks: Holding a DB transaction open across network I/O ties up connections and row locks; a broker stall stalls the relay and can pile up idle-in-transaction sessions
Out-of-order publication for the same order key when two relays claim different rows of the same aggregate
Silent event loss if published_at is set before acks, or duplicate storms/misordering if retry logic re-sends already-acked batches without idempotent claim state
Consumer dedup tables pruning or capping IDs faster than 7 days, turning at-least-once duplicates into double processing
Alert threshold (1 minute) and metrics don't cover relay crash-after-claim windows or schema drift in jsonb payloads

falsification_probe.description: Seed one table with 10k outbox rows including ~50 orders with 3+ events each; run two relay instances concurrently with a Kafka proxy injecting 500ms latency and 5% send failures; then assert per-key sequence numbers arrive strictly increasing, count rows with published_at set vs successfully acked sends, and check for rows left unclaimed after the run.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any same-key sequence inversion, or a row marked published with no corresponding ack (or an unclaimed row), falsifies the design as specified; all rows eventually published with monotonic per-key order confirms it.

result.recommendation: The proposal matches the outbox direction I independently favored and handles atomicity, rollback exclusion, at-least-once delivery, key-based ordering, retention, and alerting. Before shipping, verify one silent dependency: that the event ID written to outbox.id is fixed at insert time and reused verbatim on every retry, since consumer dedup depends entirely on it. Also confirm FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED polling runs at a comfortably sub-second interval so '1 minute' lag alert has meaningful headroom.
critical_assumptions: outbox.id doubles as the event id and is never regenerated on retry; consumers dedupe on exactly that value.
Order id used as Kafka key is present in the outbox row and stable, so per-order ordering holds across multiple relay workers and pods.
The relay's poll loop runs frequently enough (e.g., 100-500ms) that broker ack waits do not stall other rows; poll uses a bounded batch with per-message timeouts.
published_at is set only after acks=all confirmation, and the marking UPDATE cannot be lost on crash without re-publishing (duplicates tolerated).
All order-creation code paths actually run inside a Spring-managed transaction so the outbox insert shares commit/rollback with the order.
material_risks: If any code path creates orders outside the shared transaction (new async path, different datasource), outbox rows can be missing or orphaned relative to orders.
Long broker outages plus a 100-row batch with blocking acks can stall the relay; without per-send timeouts one slow broker blocks the whole poll.
Replicas all polling with SKIP LOCKED is correct, but if the poll interval is coarse (seconds) the 'oldest unpublished > 1 min' alert fires late or, conversely, flaps under normal load.

Retention job deleting rows after 7 days is safe only if published_at was set; a bug where published_at is set but Kafka write silently failed would make the event permanently lost and invisible to the alert (mitigated by only setting after ack).
Payload built from data outside the transaction (e.g., calling a pricing service) could still introduce non-determinism, but jsonb snapshot inside the tx avoids this.

falsification_probe.description: In a staging environment, run the relay under `kill -9` of the pod in a tight loop while orders are created, then query: `SELECT count(*) FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL AND created_at < now() - interval '5 seconds'` and compare with `SELECT count(*) FROM orders` vs Kafka message count filtered to those order ids. Also confirm consumer dedup: send the same outbox.id twice and check the fulfilment consumer's processed-id table does not double-process.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Zero committed orders without a corresponding Kafka message within a few seconds, and duplicates with identical event ids are ignored by consumers. If any committed order lacks an event, or if regenerated ids cause reprocessing, the proposal's core assumption fails.

result.recommendation: The outbox approach is correct; tighten the relay so publishing is idempotent per outbox id (set published_at only after acks, retry with backoff on failure, and prevent concurrent same-key publishes via a per-order claim or single-threaded-per-partition relay). Verify consumers dedupe on the event id, and set Kafka durability (acks=all, min.insync.replicas>=2, unclean leader election off) plus alerting on outbox lag and pending-row growth.
critical_assumptions: All three consumers truly dedupe on event id, making at-least-once safe
Consumers tolerate slight reordering/retries around a key during relay retries
Kafka topic durability configured so acks=all does not silently lose messages (min.insync.replicas>=2, unclean leader election disabled)
Polling relay runs continuously across all 6 pods and is not blocked indefinitely by a crashed claim
The outbox insert and order insert share the same DB transaction and connection
material_risks: Crash between Kafka send and published_at update causes duplicates that could trigger side effects if any consumer's dedupe is buggy or partial
Published-then-lost message under unclean leader election yields a silent gap despite acks=all
Relay downtime (all pods scaling to zero during deploy, or long GC) grows the backlog beyond acceptable lag
Retries that reorder events for the same order could be mis-handled if any consumer assumes strict per-key ordering across retries
Outbox table bloat/vacuum issues if the 7-day delete job stalls, degrading order-service write latency

falsification_probe.description: Run an integration test: (1) insert order in a transaction that rolls back and assert no outbox row; (2) commit an order, kill the relay before publish, restart, assert event arrives exactly once after dedupe; (3) simulate Kafka outage, confirm rows retry and eventually publish once per id; (4) inspect consumer dedupe by querying processed event IDs for a resent id.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If any committed order fails to produce a delivered (deduped) event, or a rolled-back order produces one, the proposal's guarantee is broken. If all paths converge to exactly-once side effects, the design holds.

result.recommendation: Keep the outbox+relay direction but specify: read the batch with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a short DB transaction, release row locks before network I/O, publish to Kafka outside that transaction, then update published_at in a new short transaction (or mark rows as IN_PROGRESS and reconcile). Add idempotent producer config (enable.idempotence=true, acks=all) and enforce per-key ordering by hashing keys to a fixed set of relay workers so two pods never publish the same order key concurrently. Also explicitly await the Kafka future before updating published_at.
critical_assumptions: All three consumers deduplicate on the outbox event ID for every event type.
All order-writing paths share one PostgreSQL database so order+outbox commit atomically.
Payload can be fully constructed at order-commit time with no post-commit enrichment.
Kafka producer idempotence and acks=all are configured so broker retries don't duplicate or reorder within a partition.
Publishing outside the short DB row-lock window keeps lock hold time below DB latency budgets.
material_risks: Publishing while still holding the SKIP LOCKED row locks (as literally written) stalls the relay on network I/O and can block subsequent polls or long transactions.
Marking published_at before awaiting the broker ack silently reintroduces the 0.05% loss the change is meant to fix.
Two pods concurrently sending the same order key reorders events for that order despite per-key Kafka ordering guarantees.
Crash between publish and published_at update yields duplicates; safe only if every consumer path truly dedups — unverified.
No backpressure/metrics detail for outbox growth if relay or cleanup job fails, causing table bloat on the primary.

falsification_probe.description: Inspect consumer code for all three services to confirm each persists and checks the event ID before processing (e.g., grep for INSERT into processed_event_ids / dedup table and confirm it precedes side effects like sending email).
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If any consumer processes events without a prior ID-based dedup check, at-least-once delivery with duplicates (inevitable under crashes between publish and mark) will cause duplicate fulfilment/emails — falsifies the proposal's core safety claim.

result.recommendation: The outbox direction is correct and matches my position; keep it, but fix two concrete gaps: publish each batch with a single Kafka producer transaction (or at minimum flush and await all futures before marking published_at) so a partial batch failure doesn't mark unsent rows, and explicitly remove/guard the in-transaction kafkaTemplate.send() path so rollback-originated events cannot recur. Also ensure only one relay instance is active or that SKIP LOCKED polling is paired with per-row claim (UPDATE ... RETURNING) so marking-after-ack is race-free across 6 replicas.
critical_assumptions: Consumers strictly dedupe on the outbox id as event id
SKIP LOCKED claim plus post-ack update is safe across 6 concurrent replicas
Broker acks are awaited before published_at is set (implicit, not stated)
Outbox payload equals the current event schema consumed downstream
No other code path publishes orders outside the outbox
material_risks: A crash between publish and published_at update republishes rows — fine only because consumers dedupe; if any consumer's idempotency store has a TTL shorter than retry horizon, duplicates leak
Batch of 100 where some sends succeed and the process dies before marking: retried rows are re-sent (acceptable) but rows marked individually without awaiting acks could be lost
7-day deletion before a stuck broker recovers could drop never-published rows if the alert isn't acted on
The old in-transaction send() path, if not removed, still emits rollback events, defeating the goal
Polling every replica with no backoff on DB/Kafka outage could stampede

falsification_probe.description: grep -rn "kafkaTemplate.send" across order-service source to confirm every order-event publish now goes through the outbox and none remains inside @Transactional methods
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Zero direct kafkaTemplate.send calls for OrderPlaced outside the relay; any hit inside a @Transactional class falsifies the fix for the rollback-originated events

cases.title: Per-request DataLoader to remove N+1 queries (sound control)

result.recommendation: The direction is sound: per-request DataLoaders with batching through existing repository functions preserve authorization and cut ~150-200 queries to ~3-6. Strengthen it by adding (a) a cross-request/cross-user isolation test proving loaders live in the per-request context, (b) a result-equivalence test asserting batched results match the original per-key results including row order and nulls for missing keys, and (c) an explicit cap/chunking strategy for the IN (...) parameter list. Also verify the repository functions actually accept array keys before committing, and record a pre-change p95 baseline so the <400 ms target is falsifiable.
critical_assumptions: Repository functions can accept arrays of keys (or can be extended internally) while reusing the exact same authorization predicates.
Context factory output is per-request in this Apollo Server 4 setup, so loaders are never shared across requests or users.
N+1 round-trip overhead dominates the 1.9 s p95; serialization and other queries in the operation are not the real bottleneck.
The auth filters for assignee, labels, and lastComment are static WHERE clauses over the batched keys, not per-row request-dependent checks.
Batch results can be mapped back to input keys order, with null for missing entries, without ambiguity.
material_risks: Loaders accidentally cached at module/singleton scope, leaking assignees/comments across users — an authorization breach, not just a perf bug.
Batch function re-implementing authorization instead of reusing it, silently loosening or tightening row-level access.
Wrong key-order mapping returning another task's lastComment or labels — silent data corruption under only a query-count test.
Unbounded IN (...) lists breaking or regressing plans when task counts grow beyond 50.
Shipping without a pre-change p95 baseline, making the <400 ms target unverifiable in staging.

falsification_probe.description: Write an integration test that runs projectDashboard twice with two different authenticated users on shared data, counting SQL statements (via knex query log or pg_stat_statements) and diffing every assignee/label/lastComment value against a reference run using the original per-key resolution.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Confirmed: ~3-6 queries per request and identical field values/order for both users, with no user A data in user B's response. Falsified: query count stays high, values/order differ from the reference, or any cross-user value appears.

result.recommendation: Keep the DataLoader direction but tighten it: (1) push the existing repository authorization predicates verbatim into the batch loaders' WHERE clause and add a cross-tenant test asserting a batch keyed by user A never returns user B's assignee/labels/comments; (2) log and assert actual p95 in staging under concurrency, not just query count, since statement count dropping does not prove 400 ms if a batched join or index is slow; (3) before rollout, EXPLAIN ANALYZE the three batch queries to confirm indexes on task_labels(task_id) and comments(task_id, created_at) exist; (4) treat the <10 query assertion as a regression guard, not as evidence the p95 target is met.
critical_assumptions: Repository authorization logic is expressible in a single WHERE clause per batch without per-row session/user lookups.
DataLoader caches are created fresh per request (context factory), not module-level.
Batch loaders return results ordered to match input keys; missing rows mapped to null without breaking downstream resolvers.
The three batched queries, at 50-key IN-lists, run in single-digit milliseconds on production data.
p95 of 1.9 s is dominated by round-trip count, not by one slow aggregate or connection-pool saturation under concurrency.
material_risks: Batch loader accidentally uses a shared/global cache or context built once, leaking rows across users — a direct authorization violation.
Batch omits a subtle authorization predicate present in the current per-row repository call, widening visibility.
Query count drops but p95 stays high because a batched lastComment query lacks an index on comments(task_id, created_at).
Ordering bug between batch results and input keys silently maps comments/labels to the wrong task.
<10 query assertion passes while p95 regression goes unnoticed in production concurrency.

falsification_probe.description: In staging with production-like data, run: (a) EXPLAIN ANALYZE the three batched queries with 50 keys; (b) load-test projectDashboard at expected concurrency and record p95 plus pg connection-pool wait time.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Each batch query < 10 ms and p95 < 400 ms with no pool-wait dominance confirms the proposal; a single batch > 50 ms or pool wait dominating p95 falsifies it and points to indexing or connection limits instead.

result.recommendation: Per-request DataLoaders are the right direction, but the proposal must pin down two things before rollout: (1) batch auth must be applied inside SQL by the existing repository predicates, not by post-filtering JS results, and (2) the batch functions must be proven to preserve key->index alignment when authorization silently drops rows (unauthorized entries become null at the correct position). Add an explicit contract test with mixed authorized/unauthorized tasks plus the query-count assertion, and confirm the repository layer actually exposes an id-list API without refactoring the authorization logic.
critical_assumptions: Row-level authorization is expressed as SQL predicates (WHERE clauses) rather than as a per-row JavaScript check after fetching, so it composes with a WHERE id IN (...) batch.
Repository functions can accept an array of ids without modifying or duplicating authorization logic (constraint: authorization must not change).
The base ~50-task query already returns task ids and the request user, so the loaders need no extra data to build keys.
Per-request context factory actually runs per request (no module-level singleton loader), so no cross-request/cross-user leakage.
The auth filter can drop individual keys from a batch, making positional ordering a correctness requirement, not a nicety.
material_risks: Index misalignment when some keys are filtered out by authorization: DataLoader returns results positionally, so a dropped row shifts every subsequent result, attaching the wrong assignee/label/comment to a task (cross-user data leak) — this violates the 'authorization must not change' constraint even if row counts look correct.

If repository functions do per-row auth in JS after fetching, batching moves that logic out of SQL and could accidentally return rows for unauthorized tasks, or the refactor could subtly alter the auth predicate.
Memoizing lastComment/labels per request could mask later auth re-evaluation if any field resolver re-checks permissions with different arguments.
The '<10 queries' test can pass while p95 stays above 400 ms if the base tasks query itself, the DB round-trip latency, or payload size dominates (the N+1 may not be the whole 1.9 s).
Labels likely span a join table; if the batch is done as one query per label layer, the count can silently exceed the threshold or reintroduce per-task queries under a fallback path.

falsification_probe.description: Integration test: seed 50 tasks where the requesting user is authorized for only ~half; run projectDashboard through Apollo context, (a) assert SQL query count <= 10, and (b) for every task, deep-compare assignee/labels/lastComment against direct single-row queries by task id, verifying no cross-task mixing and nulls exactly where unauthorized.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any field mismatch against the direct-query baseline (especially a shifted assignee on an unauthorized boundary) falsifies the batching/ordering design; count > 10 falsifies the batching claim. Matching results with <=10 queries confirms the loader contract, but a staging p95 still >=400 ms means the N+1 was not the bottleneck.

result.recommendation: The per-request DataLoader with repository delegation and a query-count test is the right core; keep it. Two changes are needed: (1) verify the batched repository calls actually re-encode the row-level authorization as SQL predicates over the whole ID set rather than re-checking per row (if the repo filters post-fetch per record, you reintroduce N work and possibly N queries); (2) the query-count assertion (<10) does not guarantee the 400ms p95 target — add a staging p95 measurement plus EXPLAIN of the batched lastComment query to confirm single-digit ms per batch, since after batching the remaining latency is per-query plan cost.
critical_assumptions: Authorization for assignee/labels/lastComment can be applied as SQL predicates on the batched IN (...) query, identical in semantics to current per-row checks.
Repository functions accept a list of IDs and return rows aligned to keys without further per-item queries.
DataLoader instances are created per request in the context factory, not module-level (otherwise cross-request/cross-user leakage).
Per-batch queries are individually fast (~few ms) with 50 keys; otherwise 3-6 queries still exceed 400ms.
lastComment aggregation (LIMIT 1 per task) is expressed in the batched SQL, not filtered in JS after fetching all comments.
material_risks: Authorization applied in JS after fetching by ID set: returns unauthorized rows into memory and still costs one query per row if the repo loops — a correctness and perf failure at once.
Module-scoped DataLoader cache shared across requests, leaking user-scoped data.
Fetched-but-filtered rows silently change which rows appear if ordering/null semantics differ from today.
Labels/comment batches without a proper index (task_id, …) make each batched query slow, missing p95 target despite fewer queries.
Query-count test passes while p95 stays high if the batched queries lack indexes or the IN-list plans poorly.

falsification_probe.description: In staging with 50-task production-like data: log every SQL statement for one projectDashboard request and EXPLAIN ANALYZE the three batched queries; then run p95 over ≥100 requests.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If statements number ≤ ~6, each plan executes in single-digit ms, and p95 < 400ms — confirmed. If any batched query plans >~50ms or any per-row query remains — falsified.

result.recommendation: Keep the per-request DataLoader direction, but explicitly require that authorization predicates be pushed into the batched WHERE clause (not applied post-fetch), that each batch function map results back to input-key order, and that an EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the base task query confirm it is not itself the p95 bottleneck. Also specify chunking for large IN lists and require a staging p95 gate (<400 ms) plus a query-count assertion before rollout. Add a data-correctness test (right user/label/comment on right task) alongside the query-count test, since ordering and authz bugs are silent.
critical_assumptions: Authorization filters are pure predicates on (user_id, row columns) that can be embedded in a single batched WHERE ... IN query without changing semantics.
Repository functions accept arrays of task/user ids, or can be extended internally without client-visible schema or policy change.
Batch functions return rows in input-key order (or are explicitly re-mapped), so labels/comments attach to the correct task.
DataLoaders are created strictly per request inside the context factory, never at module/singleton scope.
The base projectDashboard task query plus indexes are already fast enough that removing ~150 round trips alone gets p95 below 400 ms.
material_risks: Post-fetch authorization filtering instead of in-query filtering would either leak data or change policy, violating the 'authorization must not change' constraint.
Out-of-order batch results silently attach wrong assignee/labels/lastComment to tasks — correctness bug that passes a query-count test.
DataLoader accidentally instantiated at module scope or cached across requests, serving cross-user or stale data.
A slow base task query or missing index keeps p95 above 400 ms even after batching, so the goal is missed despite correct code.
Large IN lists exceeding PostgreSQL bind-parameter limits, causing runtime errors on bigger dashboards.

falsification_probe.description: In staging with production-like data, run the dashboard query with pg_stat_statements/query-log counting enabled and record (a) total SQL statements per request and (b) p95 latency of the base task query alone, before implementing the DataLoaders.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the base task query is already >~300 ms of the 1.9 s p95, batching alone cannot hit <400 ms and the proposal's premise is falsified. If it is fast and statements scale ~3-6x task count, batching should confirm the target.

result.recommendation: Per-request DataLoaders are the right approach, but the proposal assumes the existing repository functions can accept a list of ids; today they likely take a single id and run their own auth-filtered query, so they must be extended (or a new batch-aware path added) while reusing the exact same authorization predicate. Also specify that authorization failures must preserve current semantics (error vs. null) rather than silently becoming nulls, since returning null for unauthorized rows can change observable behavior. Finally, measure where the 1.9s actually goes first: if the base 50-task query or count/sub-resolvers dominate, batching child fields alone may not reach <400ms.
critical_assumptions: Repository functions can be batched (accept many ids) without altering their authorization SQL, and their auth predicate is a pure function of (task id, context user) so batching is sound.
The ~150-200 per-field queries are the dominant share of the 1.9s p95, not the base task query, counts, or DB connection pool contention.
The DataLoader-per-context-factory hook actually runs per request in Apollo Server 4 (context function is invoked per operation, not once at startup).
Returning null for missing/unauthorized rows matches current field-level behavior for these nullable fields.
Staging data volume and concurrency resemble production well enough for the p95 comparison to be meaningful.
material_risks: If any repository function keeps row-by-row auth checks, batching inside the loader still issues one query per key and the test's <10 assertion fails late.
Caching unauthorized results as null in the per-request memoization could mask an error the resolver previously threw, changing observable behavior without a schema change.
Over-batching (large IN lists) on an unindexed column or a `lastComment` join could add latency; needs a composite index check on task_id.
Per-request loaders multiply peak SQL concurrency under load if many requests batch simultaneously; pool sizing may become the new bottleneck.

falsification_probe.description: Add a temporary counter on Knex query events in a staging load test hitting projectDashboard with a 50-task project, and record total SQL statements plus p95 wall time before and after the DataLoader change.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If SQL count stays near 150-200 or p95 remains above ~800ms after batching, the batch path is not actually being used or the queries are not the bottleneck — falsifying the proposal as sufficient.

result.recommendation: The DataLoader direction is sound and matches one of my listed directions, but the claim that 'the same authorization filters apply' is the key risk and must be verified, not assumed: batch functions must push the requesting user's predicates into the WHERE clause of the IN query, not filter post-fetch. Add an explicit test that a user without access gets zero rows for unauthorized tasks even when those task IDs are in the batch keys, plus a p95 benchmark under concurrent load rather than a single-request query count alone. Also confirm IN-list parameter limits and add a fallback chunking if page sizes grow.
critical_assumptions: Repository authorization is expressible as SQL predicates that survive an IN (...) batch form
Batch results filtered post-fetch would be detected by existing tests (likely not true)
No cross-request cache is introduced inadvertently (e.g., shared loader instances)
Query count is actually the dominant component of the 1.9s p95
Per-request user context is reliably available in the context factory
material_risks: Post-fetch filtering instead of SQL pushdown could leak rows or subtly change counts if a downstream consumer reads raw loader output
Shared/global DataLoader instances would cache across users, causing authorization leakage
IN-list with large task sets hitting parameter limits or degraded plans
Under concurrent load, pool contention may still cap p95 even at ~10 queries
Silent ordering/identity mismatches if loaders key on non-unique fields (e.g., duplicate labels)

falsification_probe.description: Add a test that builds a DataLoader batch for task IDs spanning both authorized and unauthorized tasks for a restricted user, and assert the SQL WHERE clause contains the authorization predicate and that returned rows exclude unauthorized tasks; plus a script issuing 50 concurrent dashboard queries and measuring p95.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If unauthorized rows appear or SQL lacks the user predicate, the proposal leaks; if p95 stays above 400ms at ~10 queries/request, query count was not the dominant cause and the direction is insufficient.

result.recommendation: Per-request DataLoader with the existing repositories is the right direction, but first confirm the repository functions actually accept an array of keys and apply the same row-level authorization predicate in the batched query (if they only expose single-key lookups, batching inside them must be added without altering auth semantics). Also ensure the returned-null-for-missing behavior matches today's semantics: if an unauthorized assignee currently yields an error or a field omission rather than null, that would be a client-visible behavior change, violating the constraints. Add an index check (EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the WHERE ... IN queries for labels/comments by task_id) and re-measure p95 afterwards, since batching reduces query count but may not alone bring 1.9 s under 400 ms if the base query, serialization, or missing indexes dominate.
critical_assumptions: Repository functions can be batched (accept key arrays) while preserving the exact authorization predicate applied today.
Returning null for unauthorized/missing rows matches current field-resolution behavior and is not a schema/authorization-visible change.
The ~150-200 SQL round-trips are the dominant cost of the 1.9 s p95, not the base tasks query, serialization, or missing indexes.
Context factory runs per request (no sharing across concurrent requests), so DataLoader memoization cannot leak one user's data to another.
Batched IN queries on task_id / user_id are covered by existing indexes.
material_risks: Batching repository calls without verifying their auth filter reproduces it could silently weaken or change row-level authorization.
Mapping unauthorized rows to null instead of the current behavior (error/field omission) is a client-visible contract change, violating the no-schema-change constraint.
Empty batch edge case: DataLoader never calls the batch fn with an empty array, but a naive implementation may issue 'WHERE id IN ()' if it does.
If results are grouped rather than returned positionally, misaligned keys assign the wrong comment/labels to a task — data-integrity bug across users' dashboards.
Even at ~4-5 queries per request, p95 may stay above 400 ms if the primary tasks query itself is slow or N is much larger than 50 under load.

falsification_probe.description: Run the proposed <10-query count test plus a staging p95 benchmark on production-like data, and log EXPLAIN ANALYZE for each batched IN query.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Confirm: SQL count per request drops to single digits AND p95 < 400 ms AND the batched queries show index scans (no seq scans). Falsify: query count drops but p95 stays >= 400 ms (points to base query/serialization) or any batched query seq-scans a large table.

result.recommendation: Keep the per-request DataLoader direction, but add three concrete guardrails before rollout: (1) a differential test asserting batched results are identical to per-row results for the same user, including authorization-filtered rows; (2) an explicit assertion that batch functions preserve input key order and return null for missing keys, plus a check that loaders are created in the context factory, never module scope; (3) verify the base task-list query and index coverage on task_id/assignee_id/comment FK, since if the base fetch dominates p95 the loaders alone will not reach 400 ms. If the query-count test passes but p95 stays high, escalate to the single-query/JSONB aggregation direction.
critical_assumptions: Repository authorization predicates are pure row-level filters that hold unchanged when rewritten as WHERE id IN (...).
Apollo context factory runs exactly once per request and its object reaches all resolvers.
Postgres indexes support the batched IN (...) queries at production data volume.
Batch functions return exactly one row per key in input order, with null for missing keys.
p95 is dominated by query round-trips, not by the base task query or serialization.
material_risks: Batch ordering bug silently serves another row's assignee/lastComment (wrong data shown to user).
Authorization filter partially lost in the batched query, exposing rows the per-row path would deny.
Loaders accidentally shared across requests/users, leaking data between sessions.
p95 remains above 400 ms because the base task fetch or an unindexed IN(...) dominates, making the change a non-answer to the objective.
Multiple-rows-per-task fields (labels, comments) collapsed to a single row by the loader contract.

falsification_probe.description: Run one authenticated projectDashboard request against a production-like staging dataset with pg_stat_statements enabled (or log statements), then compare: total statement count, total DB time for the request, and p95 across ~50 requests before and after the change; also diff batched vs per-row results for the same user on a fixture where some rows are authorization-denied.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If statement count drops to <10 but total DB time and p95 stay near baseline, the round-trip hypothesis is wrong and the proposal fails. If any row differs between batched and per-row results, authorization or ordering is broken and the proposal must be revised.

cases.title: Incremental billing refactor with characterisation tests and shadow run (sound control)

result.recommendation: Keep the overall direction (golden tests → interface → shadow mode → per-plan flags), but add three things: (1) validate golden-test fidelity in the first sprint by replaying stored inputs and comparing to stored invoices — this gates everything; (2) verify the single choke point actually intercepts all line-item generation across all 5 services before committing to the design, and build a differential/property-test harness alongside golden tests to cover edges real inputs don't exercise; (3) add an explicit per-plan deletion deadline so the dual-implementation window and feature flags can't accumulate indefinitely.
critical_assumptions: Stored 18 months of inputs replay deterministically to the stored outputs through today's code
A single interface can intercept all line-item generation across all 5 services
Shadow mode can run without side effects on tax/payments/notifications (mockable or idempotent calls)
Plans can be feature-flagged individually without shared proration branches leaking across them
Other teams' ~40 PRs/week won't invalidate shadow baselines or golden snapshots mid-refactor
material_risks: Shared mutable BillingContext leaks state between shadow and real computations, corrupting both diffs and real invoices
Golden tests snapshot existing bugs, turning today's defects into immovable requirements
Grandfathered plans deferred so long that team knowledge of their proration rules is lost
Long-lived dual implementations drift; fixes applied to one path not the other
Diff-rate-zero criterion masks shared-assumption bugs where both implementations are wrong identically

falsification_probe.description: First-sprint gate: replay the stored 18 months of invoice inputs through current code and diff outputs against the stored invoices; separately, trace all call sites where invoicing requests line items and confirm they route through one interceptable seam.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If replayed outputs do not match stored invoices (non-determinism, hidden inputs, external state), or line-item generation spans multiple non-unifiable seams, the proposal's foundation fails → REPLACE. If both check out → confirms MODIFY-level tweaks are sufficient and direction is sound.

result.recommendation: The staged approach (golden tests -> interface -> shadow mode -> per-plan flags) is sound, but add three things: (1) make shadow-mode diffs deterministic by pinning clock, tax-rate lookups, and payment-provider responses per invoice, otherwise zero-diff is unmeasurable; (2) define numeric tolerance and canonicalization for the diff check (rounding order, decimal vs float, line-item ordering) before starting, and treat any nonzero diff as blocking; (3) account for the ~40 PRs/week merge traffic by gating legacy-path deletion behind an owner check and by adding contract tests on the BillingContext surface so concurrent PRs cannot silently change inputs the golden tests rely on.
critical_assumptions: Stored 18 months of invoice inputs are complete and replayable (no external lookups, tax API calls, or clock reads required at replay time)
The golden snapshots are byte-for-byte reproducible across environments, i.e. output is deterministic given inputs
Grandfathered plans' current behavior is fully represented within that 18-month window (no older, unexercised proration branches)
A per-plan feature flag cleanly partitions billing behavior, i.e. no cross-plan or shared-code paths
Shadow mode can run in production without additional cost/latency or exposing duplicate invoice data to downstream services
material_risks: Golden tests bless today's bugs: if legacy proration has known-wrong edge cases, the snapshot locks them in and the new model cannot fix them without failing the safety net
Non-determinism in shadow mode (timestamps, tax service responses, rounding order) produces perpetual diffs, stalling every plan behind an unachievable 'zero for two cycles' bar
Concurrent PRs from other teams mutate shared BillingContext or proration code mid-migration, invalidating golden snapshots and flag behavior simultaneously
Partial rollout leaves two calculators live long-term; grandfathered plans 'move last' may mean never, so legacy code and its test burden persist indefinitely
18-month replay may not cover rare proration paths (mid-cycle upgrades, credits, plan switches) that only fire annually or on specific anniversary dates

falsification_probe.description: Run the golden-test replay harness twice against the full 18-month dataset in two different environments/CI runners and diff the snapshot outputs; then inject one deliberate mutation (e.g. change a proration rounding rule) and confirm the snapshots fail.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the two runs differ even once, or if the mutation does not cause a snapshot failure, the safety net cannot support the migration and the proposal's foundation is wrong. Identical runs plus a caught mutation confirms it.

result.recommendation: Keep the replay-first strangler structure (golden tests → interface → shadow mode → per-plan flags → delete legacy, grandfathered last), but add two things: (1) define the new domain model explicitly as plan-as-data with CI-validated config and onboarding tooling, otherwise the stated goal of 'plans in days' is unmet even if the refactor succeeds; (2) replace the fixed 'zero diffs for two billing cycles' gate with a volume-based threshold, since low-volume and annual plans would otherwise stall for months or a year.
critical_assumptions: Invoice computation is deterministic: identical stored inputs yield identical outputs across runs (mutable BillingContext, timestamps, tax-service calls, and random IDs would break this)
Stored invoice inputs capture every dependency of the computation, including external tax/payment responses
There is a single, or enumerable, call site where invoicing requests line items across all 5 services
Shadow mode runs can be executed without customer-visible side effects (no payment, notification, or tax-registry side effects from the second computation)
Shadow traffic volume per plan is high enough to reach statistical confidence within a reasonable window
material_risks: Non-deterministic replay makes shadow diff rates noise; the zero-diff gate either never passes or passes spuriously, and grandfathered plans are the ones most likely to be low-volume or annual
Shadow computation accidentally triggering notification/payment side effects would bill or email real customers twice
Golden tests snapshot current code output rather than validating against actually-issued stored outputs, so pre-existing bugs get canonized as 'correct' without anyone noticing
During dual-run, a bug fix applied only to one path reintroduces divergence silently
Without a plan-as-data requirement and onboarding tooling, the team delivers an engine but plans still take weeks because each new plan needs custom code and review

falsification_probe.description: Select 100 randomly chosen stored invoices spanning all 37 plans (including grandfathered), replay each twice through today's code in separate fresh processes with fresh BillingContext objects, and diff the two runs' outputs.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Zero diffs across all 200 runs confirms determinism and makes shadow-mode diffing a valid gate; any nonzero diff rate means shadow diffs will be dominated by noise, falsifying the proposal's central validation criterion before any refactor begins.

result.recommendation: Keep the golden-test -> interface -> shadow mode -> per-plan flag sequence, but add three things: (1) make shadow computation use an isolated, deep-copied BillingContext so legacy runs are never mutated; (2) time-box and explicitly budget dual maintenance, with a hard cap on shadow duration and a defined owner for parity diffs; (3) pair the new domain model with a declarative plan-configuration layer so the days-not-weeks goal is met structurally, not just by having cleaner code. Also define the diff-classification policy (nondeterminism, rounding, known legacy bugs) before shadowing starts.
critical_assumptions: A single line-item seam exists or can be extracted without redesigning invoicing
Replaying stored inputs reproduces current outputs exactly (inputs complete, code deterministic)
Shadow mode can be made side-effect-free across tax, payments, and notifications
Per-plan feature flags are enforceable consistently across all 5 services
Golden snapshots capture the real proration edge cases, not just the 22% happy paths
material_risks: Shared mutable BillingContext leaks state between shadow and real runs, contaminating live invoices or producing false diffs that mask real divergence
Shadow mode becomes permanent: two implementations live indefinitely while 40 PRs/week land on both
Golden tests snapshot legacy bugs as correct, so the new model either preserves defects or fails parity on rare grandfathered proration paths
A plan cutover leaves services disagreeing (flag applied inconsistently), generating wrong invoices for a real customer
Reproducibility fails for stored inputs, collapsing the parity evidence base and forcing a fallback to hand-written tests

falsification_probe.description: Pick ~500 stored invoices across at least 5 plan types (including 2 grandfathered) and replay their inputs through current main in a hermetic script; diff outputs field-by-field against the stored results. In the same pass, assert the code path from invoice request to line items crosses a single modifiable call site.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any nonzero diff, or discovery that line-item generation spans multiple unconnected call sites across services, falsifies the core premise (reproducible golden tests + one seam) and would push toward a rules-engine or heavier seam extraction first. Zero diffs and one seam confirms the proposal is viable.

result.recommendation: The direction matches my preferred approach (replay oracle + seam + shadow mode + grandfathered-last) and is sound. Three additions: (1) make the golden replay harness a permanent CI regression suite, not a one-time snapshot, so later 40-PRs/week merges are guarded; (2) explicitly handle the mutable shared BillingContext — the proposal leaves the cross-service coupling that motivated the refactor untouched, so snapshot the context at the seam and forbid mutation across it; (3) state how a new plan becomes deployable — a calculator interface alone still requires code changes, so plan definitions must land in config/registry form or 'days not weeks' is not achieved.
critical_assumptions: Stored 18 months of invoice inputs are sufficient and deterministic to reproduce issued invoices (no hidden external state, clocks, or tax-service nondeterminism).
There exists a single point where invoicing requests line items for all 37 plans, so one interface covers every path including grandfathered ones.
Production can afford dual computation of every invoice (CPU/latency) and diff logging without customer impact.
Per-plan feature flags can be applied without coordinated multi-service deploys.
Two full billing cycles of zero-diff is an acceptable schedule cost for the team of 3.
material_risks: Golden snapshots enshrine existing bugs; if anyone 'fixes' a discrepancy during migration, grandfathered invoices silently change — diffs must be treated as ground truth, not bugs.
Shadow-mode diff noise from tax/rounding/timing makes a real regression indistinguishable from benign variance, stalling migration or masking breakage.
BillingContext remains mutable and shared across 5 services; concurrent PRs from other teams can change inputs between the two calculator paths or after flags flip.
Legacy code deletion per plan while other teams still merge against those paths causes merge conflicts or accidental reactivation.
Two-cycle verification per plan across 37 plans serializes the timeline; parallelizing per-plan flags needs explicit sequencing to avoid feedback cycles.

falsification_probe.description: Take one stored month of real invoice inputs, run them through today's code twice in separate clean environments/CI runs, and diff the outputs byte-for-byte (including rounding, tax lines, timestamps).
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Byte-identical outputs confirm the replay-oracle premise and the whole golden-test strategy. Any nondeterminism (clock, randomness, external service, ordering) falsifies the snapshot approach and forces a normalized comparison or recorded-fixtures design before proceeding.

result.recommendation: Keep the overall strategy, but change the golden-test step: replaying stored inputs through *today's* code only proves the refactor matches current behavior, not the invoices customers actually received. Also replay against the stored issued-invoice outputs and triage any mismatches, since 6 years of proration changes mean some historical paths no longer reproduce. Additionally, make shadow-mode computation use deep-cloned inputs per implementation — the shared mutable BillingContext will cause the two calculators to corrupt each other's state and produce false diffs.
critical_assumptions: Stored invoice inputs are complete and deterministic enough to be replayed (no external calls, clock, or randomness dependence) — needs verification, not assumption.
Today's code reproduces the 18 months of actually-issued invoices; otherwise the golden baseline is wrong from day one.
Shadow mode can run both calculators in-process on cloned BillingContext state without cross-contamination or doubling production latency/cost beyond acceptable limits.
A per-plan feature flag can cleanly gate the single BillingCalculator call site — i.e., plan identity is available at that point.
Long-lived per-plan flags remain mergeable against ~40 PRs/week touching these services for multiple billing cycles.
material_risks: Baseline built from current code silently freezes existing bugs as 'expected' output; conversely, if current code already diverges from issued invoices, the whole equivalence claim collapses.
Shared mutable BillingContext lets shadow executions interfere, producing either false diffs (wasted cycles) or masked real diffs (missed regressions).
Golden tests at ~22% coverage will mostly capture happy paths; proration edge cases (mid-cycle upgrades, partial months, grandfathered rules) are where divergence hides.
Golden snapshots become brittle and get blindly updated under 40 PRs/week merge pressure, defeating their purpose.
Moving grandfathered plans last means the highest-risk, hardest-to-verify plans sit behind flags longest, accumulating flag debt and drift.

falsification_probe.description: Take a stratified sample (e.g. 200 invoices across all 37 plans, including edge cases) from the 18-month store, recompute line items with today's code, and diff against the stored issued invoice outputs.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Zero mismatches confirms the current code is a valid golden baseline. Any mismatch (especially clustered by proration rule or plan era) falsifies the assumption that replaying inputs through today's code yields correct golden values, and the baseline must instead be anchored to stored outputs.

result.recommendation: Keep the golden-test and shadow-mode strategy, but first run a replay feasibility spike over the stored 18 months of invoices to verify every input (especially mutable BillingContext fields) was persisted and outputs are deterministic; the whole plan rests on that. Also re-scope the 'new domain model' to a declarative plan/proration configuration behind BillingCalculator rather than a broad rewrite — the objective is fast plan authoring, not a clean-room model — and add a rollback story for the per-plan flags plus a merge-freeze/coordination tactic for the ~40 external PRs/week touching these services.
critical_assumptions: Stored 18 months of invoice inputs include every field the current code reads (mutable BillingContext, time, tax rates, feature state) and are sufficient to reproduce outputs deterministically
Current code is deterministic given stored inputs (no wall-clock, randomness, or external calls that changed)
Shadow mode can run both implementations without double-charging, and diffs can be attributed to a plan cheaply
Per-plan feature flags can be enforced at the single BillingCalculator call site with no other code paths bypassing it
Grandfathered-plan behaviour is fully captured by the 18-month window (plans older than 18 months may not have recent invoices)
material_risks: If stored inputs are incomplete or non-deterministic, golden tests will fail at baseline and the entire verification strategy collapses with no fallback oracle
Silent divergence in tax/rounding/proration edge cases that only appear on rare invoice shapes the shadow mode never sees before cutover
External PRs merged during the long migration window can change legacy code after it is golden-tested, invalidating baselines and creating flag-vs-flag bugs
Zero-diff-rate gate may never trigger for low-volume plans, stalling the migration indefinitely
Deleting legacy paths per plan before all rollback windows close removes the only comparison oracle mid-migration

falsification_probe.description: Build a minimal replay harness that runs today's code over a random sample of ~1,000 stored invoices and byte-compares emitted line items/totals to the stored originals.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If >99% reproduce exactly (modulo known volatile fields), the golden-test foundation holds; if a material fraction differ or inputs are missing, the proposal's core verification mechanism is unworkable and must be redesigned first.

result.recommendation: Keep the golden-replay + interface-seam + shadow-mode + per-plan-flag plan, but add three explicit provisions: (1) define parity scope as invoice line items and totals only, excluding tax/payment/notification side effects, else shadow mode will produce unactionable diffs; (2) make the seam pass an immutable snapshot rather than the shared mutable BillingContext, or the new calculator will inherit nondeterminism and shadow diffs will be noise; (3) hard-cap shadow compute cost (sample or async) and set a written deletion date for each legacy path so per-plan flags do not become permanent dual implementations.
critical_assumptions: Stored invoice inputs are complete and deterministic enough that replaying them through current code reproduces stored outputs byte-for-byte or within a defined tolerance.
Shadow-mode diffs can be computed without double-charging tax/payment/notification services or requiring 2x invoice compute budget.
A single seam (BillingCalculator) actually covers every line-item source across the 5 services, not just the invoicing service's happy path.
Per-plan feature flags can be flipped independently without entangling shared proration code used by multiple plans.
Grandfathered plans' rule versions are recoverable from stored data so they can be validated last with the same harness.
material_risks: Replay harness fails immediately because tax rates/FX/run-order are not persisted, stalling the whole program at step one.
Shadow mode runs against real payment/tax integrations and causes duplicate side effects or cost blowups.
Mutable BillingContext leaks across the seam, producing nondeterministic diffs that get either ignored or chased indefinitely.
